title: Два выходных для Лёвы и визит к Нагиеву  (Two Days Off for Lyova and Visiting Nagiyev)

segments.t: Handing Lyova tickets to Saint Petersburg, Chef Barinov declares that his sous-chef is officially on a two-day holiday and orders him to take his mother on the trip immediately. Meanwhile, Max spots Nagiyev heading into his office and decides to ask the owner for a loan.
А сейчас начался у тебя выходной.
Alright, let's go through it step by step in English.
'But I am on shift at work.' Barinov highlights one concrete touch for Lyova: "rabote" means "work" (from "rabota"), giving the line its exact edge.
'You were, Lyova.' Max sends this line on cue: spoken Russian trims this down to just 2 words, dropping the extra helper words that English has to spell out.
А сейчас начался у тебя выходной.
'Right now your day off has officially started.' Lyova chimes in pointedly to be clear, watching Barinov's face to see how the news lands.
'Or rather, two days off.' Barinov centers this vivid choice in earnest: "vykhodnykh" means "weekend" (from "vykhodnoy"), giving the line its exact edge.

'Wait, what about the carrots?' Max phrases this statement to Barinov: putting the question word "kak" right at the front of the line lets Barinov hear the point of the question on the very first beat.
'Come on, hurry up and get going.' Lyova answers openly across the room, to clear the air between them once and for all.
'What else now?' Barinov chooses one sharp expression toward Lyova: "yeshchyo" means "more, still", and it carries the main weight of what Barinov is saying.
'You wound me, Lyova.' Max makes the thought without fuss: spoken Russian trims this down to just 2 words, dropping the extra helper words that English has to spell out.
'We are just hanging out here.' Lyova speaks right away without a pause, watching Barinov's face to see how the news lands.
'Ah, you are heading in there.' Barinov brings the thought before Max: notice how Russian needs no word for "am", "is", or "are" in the present — placing the words side by side says it all.

'There is the man I should borrow money from.' Max states the comment calmly now: the single Russian word "nado" ("it is necessary, one needs to") sets up the whole statement without needing a separate word for "it is".
'So you got all that, Dmitry Vladimirovich?' Lyova probes sharply in front of Max without any preamble.
'What do you want?' Barinov leans on this vivid word in earnest: "nado" means "it is necessary", and it carries the main weight of what Barinov is saying.
А сейчас начался у тебя выходной.
That wraps up this scene as chef Barinov gives Lyova two days off and sends him to Saint Petersburg with his mother, while Max decides to ask Nagiyev for an advance. Until next time!
